content: An endometrial polyp, also known as a uterine polyp, is a growth or lesion that develops in the lining of the uterus, called the endometrium. These polyps occupy space within the uterine cavity and are relatively common, affecting up to 10% of women. They can either have a broad, flat base (sessile) or be attached to the uterine wall by a thin, elongated stalk (pedunculated). Pedunculated polyps are more frequently observed than sessile ones. The size of these polyps can vary significantly, ranging from a few millimeters to several centimeters. In cases where the polyp is pedunculated, it may extend through the cervix and into the vagina. Larger polyps may contain small blood vessels, which can contribute to symptoms. The exact cause of endometrial polyps is not definitively known, but they are believed to be influenced by hormonal levels, particularly circulating estrogen, which stimulates their growth. Many polyps are asymptomatic, but when symptoms do occur, they may include irregular menstrual bleeding, bleeding between menstrual periods, excessively heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), and vaginal bleeding after menopause. Bleeding from the blood vessels within the polyp can lead to increased blood loss during menstruation, spotting between periods, or postmenopausal bleeding. If a polyp protrudes through the cervix into the vagina, it may cause pain, a condition known as dysmenorrhea. Endometrial polyps can be diagnosed using various methods, including vaginal ultrasound (sonohysterography), hysteroscopy, or dilation and curettage. However, detection via ultrasound can be challenging, especially in the presence of endometrial hyperplasia, which is an excessive thickening of the endometrium. Larger polyps may also be missed during curettage procedures. Power Doppler imaging can sometimes reveal a feeding blood vessel within the polyp, aiding in diagnosis. Treatment for endometrial polyps typically involves surgical removal, either through curettage or hysteroscopy. Curettage carries a risk of missing polyps, so the uterus may first be explored with grasping forceps to minimize this risk. Hysteroscopy allows direct visualization of the polyp, which can then be removed through the cervix. For larger polyps, they may need to be sectioned into smaller pieces before removal. If cancerous cells are identified within the polyp, a hysterectomy may be performed. However, hysterectomy is generally not considered unless malignancy is confirmed. Surgical removal of polyps is usually performed under general anesthesia. Endometrial polyps are most often benign, but a small percentage (approximately 5%) may contain precancerous or cancerous cells, such as adenocarcinoma. These polyps can also increase the risk of miscarriage in women undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatment. If polyps develop near the openings of the fallopian tubes, they may interfere with fertility and make it more difficult to conceive. While treatments like hysteroscopy are effective in removing the polyps, recurrence is common. Endometrial polyps are most frequently observed in women in their 40s and 50s. Risk factors for developing these polyps include obesity, high blood pressure, and a history of cervical polyps. The use of medications such as tamoxifen or hormone replacement therapy can also increase the likelihood of uterine polyps. It is estimated that endometrial polyps are present in up to 10% of women and in approximately 25% of women experiencing abnormal vaginal bleeding. Structurally, endometrial polyps can occur as solitary growths or in clusters. They are typically round or oval in shape and range in size from a few millimeters to several centimeters in diameter. Their color is usually similar to the surrounding endometrium, appearing red or brown, although larger polyps may appear darker red. These polyps are composed of dense fibrous tissue (stroma), blood vessels, and gland-like spaces lined with endometrial epithelium. Pedunculated polyps are attached to the uterine wall by a thin stalk, while sessile polyps are connected by a flat base. Pedunculated polyps are more commonly observed than sessile ones.
